blocks.heading: Reasons people work
blocks.text: People work for income to meet living needs, security, social contact, recognition, achievement and opportunities to develop their abilities. Different people place different weight on these rewards, and priorities can change. Work can support needs without satisfying all of them: a well-paid job may be insecure or isolating. Job security means confidence that employment will continue. Social security concerns protection or benefits against specified risks, rather than simply keeping the same job. Do not substitute one meaning for the other. An employer choosing a motivation approach needs evidence of staff needs, not an assumption that everyone wants the same thing.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: At fictional Omi Foods one worker values reliable earnings while another values learning a more responsible role. A pay rise may appeal to the first worker, while greater responsibility may better address the second worker’s stated need. The employer should still check whether the work and basic conditions are acceptable.

blocks.heading: Keeping the ideas apart
blocks.text:
Explain the difference between job security and social security. A fictional worker expects her employment to continue; a separate benefit arrangement protects eligible workers against a specified income risk.

The expectation of continued employment is job security. The benefit arrangement is social security or protection. Confidence about keeping a job does not itself describe a benefit or insurance arrangement.
